concept.name: Moneyness
concept.definition: Moneyness is the position of an underlying asset's price relative to an option's strike price, classifying the option as in-the-money (positive intrinsic value if exercised now), at-the-money (strike equals the current price), or out-of-the-money (zero intrinsic value). It can be measured against spot or against the forward price, and quantified numerically, e.g., by log-moneyness or by the option's delta.
concept.intuition: Moneyness tells you whether an option would be worth anything if it expired right now, and roughly how much 'cushion' it has.
concept.mechanics: Simple moneyness is S/K (or its reciprocal); log-moneyness is ln(F/K); standardized moneyness divides ln(F/K) by sigma*sqrt(T) to express moneyness in standard deviations. Calls are ITM when S > K, puts when S < K. Delta is a common practical proxy for percent moneyness.
concept.formula: Simple moneyness M = F/K (or S/K); standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K) / (sigma*sqrt(T)), where F is the forward price, K the strike, sigma implied volatility, T time to expiry.
concept.failure_modes: Spot-based moneyness misclassifies options when carry is large (high rates or dividends); forward-based (ATMF) classification is then more meaningful. Delta-as-moneyness breaks down for long-dated or high-volatility options where delta diverges from the risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM.
concept.misconceptions: Moneyness is not a statement about profitability of the position — an ITM long option can still be a losing trade if the premium paid exceeds the intrinsic value realized. 'At-the-money' in practice usually means nearest strike, not exact equality.
concept.example: With stock at $100, the $95 call is in-the-money by $5, the $100 call is at-the-money, and the $105 call is out-of-the-money; for puts the relationship is reversed.
